passages.text: One promising approach to overcoming these challenges is the development of simultaneous multiple interaction t-cell Engagers (SMITEs). SMITEs represent an innovative subclass of bispecific antibodies designed to augment the performance of traditional BiTEs. Structurally, SMITEs consist of two distinct BiTE molecules, each targeting specific epitopes. One BiTE is engineered to target a tumor-associated antigen (TAA) alongside CD3, while the other is focused on engaging CD28, which may target the same or a different antigen. This multi-targeting approach can increase the specificity of BsAbs and mitigate the risk of immune evasion by tumors.

Additionally, combining BsAbs with other therapies, such as checkpoint inhibitors, chemotherapy, or targeted therapies, can address the challenge posed by tumor heterogeneity and enhance treatment efficacy. This combination strategy ensures more comprehensive tumor cell clearance.
Immunogenicity

Immunogenicity is a significant concern in the development of bispecific antibodies (BsAbs) due to their heterogeneous nature. Patients may develop immune responses against these therapies, leading to reduced therapeutic efficacy and potential adverse reactions. The immune system can recognize the foreign elements of BsAbs, such as non-human sequences or novel structural configurations, triggering the production of anti-drug antibodies (ADAs). These ADAs can neutralize the therapeutic antibodies or accelerate their clearance from the body, thereby diminishing their clinical benefits.

Reducing immunogenicity is crucial for the clinical success of BsAbs and other alternative high-affinity protein-binding scaffolds that incorporate non-human sequences. Several strategies have been developed to minimize the immunogenic potential of these therapies.
Humanization of Antibodies

By modifying the antibody sequences to more closely resemble human proteins, the risk of immunogenicity can be reduced. This involves grafting the antigen-binding regions of a non-human antibody onto a human antibody framework, resulting in chimeric or humanized antibodies that are less likely to be recognized as foreign by the patient's immune system.
Use of "Inert" IgG Isotypes

Selecting IgG isotypes that are less likely to provoke an immune response can help mitigate immunogenicity. These "inert" isotypes are engineered to avoid interaction with immune cells that could trigger adverse reactions, thereby enhancing the safety profile of the BsAbs.
Screening for Low Immunogenic Potential

Meticulously screening monoclonal antibody (mAb) candidates to ensure they have lower immunogenic potential is another effective approach. This involves using advanced computational tools and in vitro assays to predict and evaluate the immunogenicity of antibody candidates before clinical development.
Deimmunization Techniques

Employing deimmunization techniques, such as epitope removal or modification, can further reduce the immunogenicity of BsAbs. By identifying and modifying specific amino acid sequences that are recognized by the immune system, the overall immunogenic profile of the antibody can be improved.
Tissue Penetration

For solid tumors, the efficacy of BsAbs significantly hinges on their ability to navigate and penetrate the complex tumor microenvironment (TME). An inflamed TME, characterized by interferon-gamma signaling, is associated with favorable clinical responses to immunotherapies. However, the TME of solid tumors presents considerable barriers that can impede the effectiveness of therapeutic agents, including BsAbs. These barriers are often categorized into two primary types: "immune-excluded" and "immune desert" environments.

The "immune-excluded" TME is characterized by the presence of immune cells that are unable to effectively infiltrate the tumor mass. Instead, these immune cells, such as T cells and other lymphocytes, are often found surrounding the tumor or trapped within the stroma (the connective tissue component of the tumor). Factors such as transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-beta) and other cytokines can create an immunosuppressive environment that discourages immune cell infiltration. TGF-beta, in particular, is known to inhibit T-cell function and promote the differentiation of immunosuppressive cell types like regulatory T cells (Tregs). Increased angiogenesis, or the formation of new blood vessels, is another hallmark of the immune-excluded TME. While angiogenesis supplies the tumor with necessary nutrients, it also creates a dense and disorganized vascular network that can act as a physical barrier, preventing immune cells and therapeutic agents from effectively reaching the tumor cells.

On the other hand, the "immune desert" TME is characterized by a complete or near-complete absence of immune cells within the tumor. These tumors may exhibit traits such as enhanced fatty acid metabolism, which can provide energy for rapid tumor growth and survival in a nutrient-deprived environment. Additionally, neuroendocrine characteristics may be present, further contributing to an immunosuppressive and resistant phenotype. These adaptations make it challenging for immune cells to recognize and attack the tumor, thereby limiting the efficacy of immunotherapies, including BsAbs.

To enhance the therapeutic impact of BsAbs in such challenging environments, current research explores the potential of combination therapies. These include the integration of TME-modulating agents or other immunotherapeutic approaches aimed at altering the TME to be more conducive to effective BsAb intervention. For instance, targeting TGF-beta signaling pathways can potentially reduce the immunosuppressive barrier, allowing for better penetration and function of BsAbs.
Resistance

As therapy progresses, tumor cells can develop resistance to BsAbs through various mechanisms, thereby reducing the effectiveness of the treatment. Understanding and overcoming these resistance mechanisms is critical for the sustained efficacy of BsAb therapies. Resistance mechanisms to immune-based therapies arise from multiple factors, including tumor-intrinsic factors, the TME, and prior treatment-related immune suppression.

Tumor-intrinsic factors contributing to resistance include genetic mutations, loss of tumor antigen expression, changes in the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) molecules, and the expression of immune checkpoints. Tumor cells may downregulate the expression of TAAs that BsAbs target, reducing their visibility to the immune system. Alterations in MHC molecules, which present antigens on the surface of tumor cells, can impair T-cell recognition. These changes can result from genetic mutations or epigenetic modifications that affect MHC expression or function. Additionally, tumor cells can evade the immune system by expressing immune checkpoint proteins, such as PD-L1, which inhibit T-cell activity.

The TME-induced resistance may involve both cellular components (Tregs, myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs), tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs), particularly the M2 phenotype) and secreted factors (IL-10, TGF-beta, COX2, and PGE2). These elements collectively create an immunosuppressive environment that hampers the effectiveness of BsAb therapies.
To counteract these resistance mechanisms, advanced combinatorial treatments are being explored.
Production and Cost

The production of BsAbs presents challenges due to their complex structure, which often requires sophisticated manufacturing processes. BsAbs are typically composed of two different antibody fragments, which need to be correctly assembled and maintained in a stable configuration. This complexity not only makes the production process more intricate but also increases the risk of manufacturing errors and product inconsistencies.

Developing more efficient and cost-effective production methods is crucial for making BsAb therapies more widely available. Strategies to achieve this can be explored, including optimizing cell lines and expression systems, streamlining purification processes, and exploring alternative production platforms such as microbial fermentation.

The future of solid tumors BsAbs lies in the development of more specific, effective, and adaptable therapeutic strategies that can overcome the challenges posed by tumor complexity and heterogeneity. Numerous innovative strategies are being explored to enhance the application and effectiveness of BsAbs in treating solid tumors, including bispecific T-cell engaging receptors (TCERs), BiTE-armed oncolytic viruses, BsAb-armed CAR-T cells, etc. Through continued research and innovation, BsAbs have the potential to significantly improve outcomes for patients with solid tumors.
Conclusion

The landscape of cancer treatment has been notably enhanced by the development and clinical integration of BsAbs, particularly in the realm of solid tumors. These innovative therapeutic agents, characterized by their ability to simultaneously target two distinct antigens, have demonstrated significant potential to overcome the limitations of traditional therapies and improve patient outcomes. The clinical success of BsAbs in hematologic malignancies has set a promising precedent for their application in solid tumors, despite the intrinsic challenges posed by the tumor microenvironment and the heterogeneity of solid malignancies.

The current generation of BsAbs targeting solid tumors, including those directed against EGFR, HER2, and PD-L1, among others, exemplifies the strides made in precision medicine. These treatments not only provide a more targeted attack on cancer cells but also engage the immune system in a more effective and regulated manner. However, the journey from bench to bedside is fraught with challenges, including overcoming the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, ensuring selective targeting to minimize off-target effects, and managing the unique toxicity profiles associated with dual targeting.

passages.text: Emerging strategies, such as combining BsAbs with other therapeutic modalities, optimizing BsAb formats for better tissue penetration and reduced immunogenicity, and leveraging novel targets within the tumor microenvironment, hold promise for enhancing the efficacy and safety of BsAbs in solid tumors. Furthermore, the exploration of personalized medicine approaches, including the use of biomarkers to predict response and tailor therapy, is critical for maximizing the therapeutic potential of BsAbs.

As we advance, the continuous evolution of BsAbs will necessitate a multidisciplinary effort encompassing innovative drug design, comprehensive preclinical testing, and adaptive clinical trial designs. The ultimate goal is to fully realize the potential of BsAbs in providing durable, effective, and safe treatments for patients with solid tumors. The progress made thus far underscores the transformative potential of BsAbs, heralding a new era in cancer therapy where precision, efficacy, and patient safety are paramount.

passages.text: Tretinoin synergistically enhances the antitumor effect of combined BRAF, MEK, and EGFR inhibition in BRAF V600E colorectal cancer
Abstract

Patients with BRAF-mutated colorectal cancer (BRAF V600E CRC) are currently treated with a combination of BRAF inhibitor and anti-EGFR antibody with or without MEK inhibitor. A fundamental problem in treating patients with BRAF V600E CRC is intrinsic and/or acquired resistance to this combination therapy. By screening 78 compounds, we identified tretinoin, a retinoid, as a compound that synergistically enhances the antiproliferative effect of a combination of BRAF inhibition and MEK inhibition with or without EGFR inhibition on BRAF V600E CRC cells. This synergistic effect was also exerted by other retinoids. Tretinoin, added to BRAF inhibitor and MEK inhibitor, upregulated PARP, BAK, and p-H2AX. When either RARalpha or RXRalpha was silenced, the increase in cleaved PARP expression by the addition of TRE to ENC/BIN or ENC/BIN/CET was canceled. Our results suggest that the mechanism of the synergistic antiproliferative effect involves modulation of the Bcl-2 family and the DNA damage response that affects apoptotic pathways, and this synergistic effect is induced by RARalpha- or RXRalpha-mediated apoptosis. Tretinoin also enhanced the antitumor effect of a combination of the BRAF inhibitor and anti-EGFR antibody with or without MEK inhibitor in a BRAF V600E CRC xenograft mouse model. Our data provide a rationale for developing retinoids as a new combination agent to overcome resistance to the combination therapy for patients with BRAF V600E CRC.

Tretinoin enhanced the antitumor effect of a combination of BRAF inhibitor and anti-EGFR antibody with or without MEK inhibitor in a BRAF V600E CRC model in vitro and in vivo. Our data provide a rationale for developing retinoids as a new combination agent to overcome resistance to the combination therapy for patients with BRAF V600E CRC.

INTRODUCTION

Activated BRAF plays an important role in cancer development and progression by regulating proliferation, differentiation, the cell cycle, angiogenesis, apoptosis, and migration. BRAF mutation occurs in various malignancies, such as melanoma, thyroid cancer, CRC, and non-small-cell lung cancer. Previous studies have proposed a BRAF mutation classification based on kinase activity, RAS dependence, and dimerization. Of the three proposed classes, BRAF V600E, a RAS-independent monomer, belongs to class 1. BRAF V600E accounts for 70%-80% of BRAF mutations in patients with CRC.

Compared with patients having BRAF-wild type CRC, those whose tumors harbor the BRAF mutation have a poor prognosis and a poor response to chemotherapy. BRAF inhibitor monotherapy is effective against BRAF-mutated melanoma or thyroid cancer. In contrast, BRAF inhibitor monotherapy has been less effective against BRAF-mutated CRC. A main mechanism of intrinsic resistance to BRAF inhibitor monotherapy in BRAF-mutated CRC is the EGFR-mediated reactivation of MAPK signaling. The addition of EGFR inhibitor to BRAF inhibitor led to overcoming the intrinsic resistance of BRAF V600E CRC to BRAF inhibitor alone in vitro and in vivo. In a randomized open-label phase III study in patients with BRAF V600E CRC, triplet therapy with ENC, BIN, and CET, and doublet therapy with ENC and CET, compared with investigators' choice of irinotecan or FOLFIRI plus CET, were associated with improved OS. However, acquired resistance to the combination therapy of BRAF inhibition and EGFR inhibition, which has been associated with various alterations in the RAS-RAF-MEK-ERK signaling pathway, is another problem for treating patients with BRAF V600E CRC. Further development of BRAF-targeted therapeutic strategies is therefore required for patients with BRAF V600E CRC.

In the present study, we aimed to identify compounds that enhance the antitumor effect of BRAF inhibitor, MEK inhibitor, and anti-EGFR antibody in BRAF V600E CRC for potential clinical application. We also aimed to clarify the underlying mechanisms of the synergistic effect between the identified compounds and BRAF-targeted therapy.
MATERIALS AND METHODS
Cell culture

CRC cell lines used in this study are listed in Table S1. Cell lines were cultured in RPMI 1640 or DMEM with 10% FBS in a humidified atmosphere with 5% CO2 in air at 37 C. Cell line authentication was performed by short tandem repeat analysis using the GenomeLab human STR primer set (Beckman Coulter, CA, USA).
Reagents

DAB, TRA and TRE, RET and TAM, BEX, and CET were purchased from LC Laboratories (Woburn, MA, USA), Cayman Chemical (Ann Arbor, MI, USA), Selleck Chemicals (Houston, TX, USA), MedChemoExpress (Monmouth Junction, NJ, USA), and Merck Serono (Tokyo), respectively. ENC and BIN were purchased from Cayman Chemical and MedChemoExpress.
Cell viability assay

Cell viability was assessed 72 h after treatment using the Cell Counting Kit-8 assay (Merck, Darmstadt, Germany) according to the manufacturer's protocol. If each drug revealed an antiproliferative effect, CI was calculated using the CompuSyn software application (version 1.0: ComboSyn, Inc., Paramus, NJ, USA). Combination effects were classified as strong synergism (CI < 0.3), synergism (CI 0.3-0.7), slight synergism/additive effect (CI 0.7-1.0), or antagonistic effect (CI > 1.0).
Screening compounds to enhance BRAF inhibitor and MEK inhibitor

We used the SCADS inhibitor kit IV, which contains 78 chemical compounds developed for other diseases, to screen compounds that might enhance the antiproliferative effect of DAB and TRA in RKO cells. Cells were incubated in 500 nM of each compound alone in the SCADS inhibitor kit or with added DAB 50 nM and TRA 5 nM for 72 h (Figure 1A). The relative cell viability of cells treated with DAB/TRA was calculated by normalization to that treated with DMSO alone in the SCADS inhibitor kit alone.

Tretinoin (TRE) was identified as promising for enhancing the antiproliferative effect of BRAF/MEK/EGFR inhibition. (A) Schematic of the screening used to identify compounds that might enhance BRAF and MEK inhibition. (B) RKO cells were treated with each SCADS inhibitor kit IV compound alone or with dabrafenib (DAB) and trametinib (TRA). Both axes represent cell viability: The horizontal, after treatment with each SCADS inhibitor kit IV compound alone; the vertical, after additional treatment with DAB/TRA. (C) Viability of various lines of BRAF V600E CRC cells treated with encorafenib (ENC), binimetinib (BIN), and TRE at various concentrations was determined. Results are presented as means +- SEM.
Cell cycle analysis

Cells were collected and washed after the treatment, fixed overnight in 70% ethanol at 4 C, and then incubated with RNase and propidium iodide. Samples were analyzed in a CytoFLEX LX flow cytometer (Beckman Coulter Life Sciences, Indianapolis, IN, USA).
Annexin V-FITC apoptosis assay

Cells were collected after the treatment, and apoptosis was detected using the Annexin V-FITC Apoptosis Detection Kit (Nacalai Tesque, Kyoto). The measurements were obtained using the CytoFLEX LX flow cytometer.
Microarray analysis

The SurePrint G3 Human Gene Expression 8 x 60 K microarray kit (version 3.0: Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA, USA) was used to identify genes that were differentially expressed by DMSO- and TRE-treated cells and by ENC/BIN- and TRE/ENC/BIN-treated cells. RKO and HT29 cells were incubated with each treatment for 24 h. After incubation, total RNA was extracted from the cells using the RNeasy Mini kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany), and labeled cRNA was prepared using standard Agilent protocols. The change multiplier was calculated for each sample using the GeneSpring software application (version 14.5: Agilent Technologies). Genes whose change multiplier was >2 were defined as altered genes. The microarray data were registered to the Gene Expression Omnibus database (GSE269880 and GSE269881; http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov.geo/).
Kinex antibody microarray

The Kinex KAM-2000 antibody microarray (Kinexus Bioinformatics Corporation, Vancouver, BC, Canada) was used to analyze the total protein including unphosphorylated and phosphorylated proteins, and phosphorylated protein expression profile of cells treated with DMSO, TRE, ENC/BIN, or TRE/ENC/BIN. RKO cells were incubated with each treatment for 48 h. After incubation, the samples were sent to the Kinexus Bioinformatics Corporation for hybridization and analysis. Proteins altered by TRE/ENC/BIN except for those altered by TRE alone and ENC/BIN were analyzed. Total proteins and phosphorylated proteins whose percentage change from control was 45 or greater, or -45 and greater, were defined as significantly changed.
Pathway analysis

Using the mRNA microarray and antibody microarray results, the Database for Annotation, Visualization, and Integrated Discovery tool (Laboratory of Human Retrovirology and Immunoinformatics, Frederick, MD, USA) was applied for pathway analyses. Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathways (Kanehisa Laboratories, Kyoto) belonging to the Environmental Information Processing and Cellular Processes categories were selected for analysis. Signaling pathways were regarded as significantly changed when they met the screening criteria (p <= 0.05) and included at least 10 genes or proteins.
Western blot analysis

Western blot analyses were performed following the standard protocol. Primary antibodies used are listed in Table S2. The band intensities were quantified by densitometry using the ImageJ software application (version 1.53a, US National Institutes of Health, Bethesda, MD, USA), and the expression of each protein was normalized to that of internal protein controls such as tubulin, GAPDH, or beta-actin.
RNA transfection

siGENOME Human RARA siRNA SMARTpool (M-003437-02-0005), siGENOME Human RXRA siRNA SMARTpool (M-003443-02-0005), and siGENOME Non-Targeting siRNA Pool (D-001206-13-05) were purchased from Horizon Discovery Ltd. (Waterbeach, Cambridge, UK). Cells were transfected with 25 nM of the siRNAs using Lipofectamine 2000 transfection reagent (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA).
Animal experiments

Each mouse received an injection of HT29 cells in DMEM mixed 1:1 with Matrigel (Corning Life Sciences, Tewksbury, MA, USA) subcutaneously into the flank region. When the tumor volume reached 150-200 mm3, mice were randomly assigned to six treatment groups: vehicle control (n = 7), TRE (n = 7), ENC/CET (n = 7), TRE/ENC/CET (n = 7), ENC/BIN/CET (n = 7), and TRE/ENC/BIN/CET (n = 7). TRE, ENC, and BIN were administered orally at doses of 10, 5, and 1.75 mg/kg, respectively, daily for 28 days. CET was administered intraperitoneally at a dose of 20 mg/kg twice weekly for 28 days. Tumor size and body weight were measured every 3 days, and the tumor volume in cubic millimeters was calculated using the formula 0.5 x length (mm) x [width (mm)].
Immunohistochemistry

Immunostaining of tumor cells with an anti-Ki-67 antibody was performed on formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tissue sections of tumors resected from mice in each group. Five fields were randomly selected using an optical microscope and imaged at x400 magnification. In each group, more than 500 tumor cells were counted, and the Ki-67 labeling index was calculated.
Statistical analyses

Statistical analyses were performed in JMP Pro (version 15.0: SAS Institute, Cary, NC, USA) and Microsoft Excel for Microsoft 365 MSO (version 2202: Microsoft Corporation, Redmond, WA, USA). Except for screening using the SCADS inhibitor kit, mRNA microarray, antibody microarray, and animal experiments, all procedures were performed as three or more independent replicates. The significance of differences between each group was estimated using the unpaired Student's t-test. Differences were considered significant when the p-value was <=0.05. Error bars are defined in the individual figures in which they appear.
RESULTS
Screening for potential compounds to enhance BRAF inhibitor and MEK inhibitor

We began with the hypothesis that certain compounds might potentiate the therapeutic efficacy of combined BRAF and MEK inhibition. To screen candidate compounds that might enhance the antiproliferative effects of DAB and TRA, we used the SCADS inhibitor kit IV. Treatment of DAB/TRA decreased the viability of the cells by 52%. Each compound in the kit was classified as a candidate compound if it, together with added DAB/TRA, decreased the viability of the cells by >20%, but alone decreased the cell viability by <20%, compared with the viability of the cells treated with DAB/TRA. TRE, a retinoid, was identified as the compound with the most promise of enhancing the efficacy of BRAF and MEK inhibitors (Figure 1B and Table S3).
TRE enhanced the antiproliferative effect of combined ENC/BIN on  BRAF V600E CRC cells

To evaluate whether TRE could synergistically enhance the antiproliferative effect of combined ENC/BIN on BRAF V600E CRC, we assessed the viability of cells cultured with ENC/BIN with or without TRE at various concentrations. TRE, at least with concentrations ranging 0.01-20 muM, was shown not to affect cell viability in NCM460, which is a normal colonic epithelial cell line. The addition of TRE to ENC/BIN resulted in a strong synergistic effect (CI < 0.3) on the RKO, HT29, Co-115, and WiDr cell lines (Figures 1C and S1; Table S4). Furthermore, the strong synergistic effect on the RKO and HT29 cells was maintained when CET was added to the TRE/ENC and the TRE/ENC/BIN combination, which are current standard regimens in clinics for patients with BRAF V600E CRC (Figures 2A and S2A-C; Tables S5 and S6). To elucidate whether enhancement of the antiproliferative effect by TRE in combination with ENC/BIN was TRE specific or common to retinoids, we performed a cell viability assay using other retinoids: RET, TAM, and BEX (Figures S3-S5; Tables S7-S9). Next, we evaluated whether TRE also synergistically enhanced the antiproliferative effect of ENC/BIN on BRAF-wild type CRC. The TRE/ENC/BIN combination did not result in a strong synergistic effect on BRAF-wild type CRC cells (Figure S6A,B; Table S10). The synergistic enhancement of retinoids was not associated with MSI status (Table S1). These results demonstrated that retinoids, including TRE, could synergistically enhance the antiproliferative effect of ENC/BIN specifically on BRAF V600E CRC cells.

Adding TRE to combined ENC and BIN induces apoptosis. (A) Viability of RKO and HT29 cells treated with TRE and ENC/BIN-cetuximab (CET) at various concentrations was determined. (B) Adding TRE to ENC/BIN increased a sub-G1 fraction of RKO cells. (C) Adding TRE to ENC/BIN increased apoptotic RKO and HT29 cells. Results are presented as means +- SEM. *p < 0.05.
TRE, when added to combined ENC/BIN, induces apoptosis in  BRAF V600E CRC cells

To clarify the mechanism of the synergistic antiproliferative effect of adding TRE to ENC/BIN, we next used flow cytometry to assess the effect of the combination on the cell cycle and induction of apoptosis. The addition of TRE to ENC/BIN was associated with a sub-G1 increase in RKO cells. In contrast, compared with ENC/BIN alone, the addition of TRE to ENC/BIN was not associated with any significant changes in the G1, S, and G2-M fractions in RKO or HT29 cells (Figure 2B). Next, when TRE was added to ENC/CET and ENC/BIN/CET, a similar tendency was observed (Figure S7A). The Annexin V-FITC assay showed that the percentage of apoptotic cells increased significantly with the addition of TRE to ENC/BIN, even though TRE alone, compared with DMSO alone, did not increase apoptotic cells (Figure 2C). In addition, we validated that TRE showed a synergistic effect of inducing apoptosis both in RKO and HT29 cells even when combined with ENC/CET and ENC/BIN/CET as well as to ENC/BIN (Figure S7B). These results indicated that adding TRE to the BRAF/MEK/EGFR inhibition induced apoptosis, one of the mechanisms of the synergistic antiproliferative effect. In addition, these results indicated that adding TRE to ENC/BIN induced apoptosis, one of the mechanisms of the synergistic antiproliferative effect.
Adding TRE to ENC/BIN was associated with altered expression of various genes and proteins involved in cell proliferation

Although TRE alone had a poor antiproliferative effect, our results revealed that the addition of TRE to ENC/BIN synergistically enhanced the antiproliferative effect. We therefore hypothesized that TRE induced different gene expression changes depending on the presence or absence of ENC/BIN. To address that hypothesis, a mRNA microarray analysis was performed using RKO and HT29 cells. With the addition of TRE to DMSO or ENC/BIN on RKO cells, 790 and 1222 genes, respectively, were judged to be significantly altered. After the same additions to HT29 cells, 1274 and 1619 genes were significantly altered. Pathway analysis indicated that the addition of TRE to ENC/BIN was associated with alterations in various genes belonging to the molecular signaling pathways involved in cell proliferation (Tables S11 and S12). Next, to elucidate whether the addition of TRE to ENC/BIN affected the expression or phosphorylation of specific proteins, we used the Kinex antibody microarray KAM-2000 to analyze the expression of total proteins including unphosphorylated and phosphorylated proteins, and phosphorylated proteins by RKO cells with each treatment (Table S13). As a result, the addition of TRE to ENC/BIN was observed to result in specific changes to 106 proteins. Pathway analysis using those proteins revealed that nine pathways were enriched with proteins belonging to molecular signaling pathways involved in cell proliferation, such as the MAPK, PI3K-Akt, FoxO, and ErbB signaling pathways (Table 1). These results indicated that TRE added to ENC/BIN is associated with alterations to many genes and proteins involved in cell proliferation. Those differences might be one of the factors underlying the synergistic antiproliferative effect of TRE/ENC/BIN.

passages.text: TRE, when added to ENC/BIN, upregulated cleaved PARP, BAK, p-H2AX

To elucidate the mechanisms involved in the enhancement of antiproliferation when TRE is added to ENC/BIN, we assessed the expression of proteins associated with cell growth. Based on the mRNA and antibody microarray results, the expression of proteins associated with the MAPK signaling pathway and the PI3K-Akt signaling pathway was assessed by western blot analysis. Our study revealed that the addition of TRE to ENC/BIN induced a level of apoptosis. Retinoids were shown to regulate Bcl-2 family proteins, leading to DNA damage and apoptosis in CRC cells. Accordingly, we assessed the expression of proteins involved in Bcl-2 apoptotic pathways or the DNA damage response. Compared with ENC/BIN alone, TRE/ENC/BIN resulted in a significant downregulation of p-MEK expression in both RKO and HT29 cells (Figures 3A and S8). However, the addition of TRE to ENC/BIN did not significantly affect the expression of p-ERK, a protein downstream of MEK (Figure 3B). Compared with ENC/BIN, TRE/ENC/BIN resulted in significant downregulation of p-AKT expression in RKO, but not in HT29 (Figures 3C and S8). TRE/ENC/BIN resulted in significant downregulation of pS6 in RKO (Figure S9). Endogenous expression of p-S6 was not detected in HT29 cells. To analyze whether TRE/ENC/BIN affected the feedback of the EGFR pathway, we also analyzed the expression of p-CRAF and p-EGFR. We found a trend in which p-CRAF was downregulated in RKO cells, but there was no endogenous expression of p-CRAF in HT29 cells (data not shown). Endogenous expression of p-EGFR was not detected in RKO and HT29 cells (data not shown). When TRE was added to ENC/BIN, cleaved PARP, BAK, and p-H2AX all significantly increased in both RKO and HT29 cells (Figures 3D,E and S8). These results suggested that the MAPK and PI3K-Akt signaling pathways were not a key part of the mechanism underlying the synergistic antiproliferative effect in all cell lines, and that the mechanism may involve modulation of the Bcl-2 family and the DNA damage response that affects apoptotic pathways.

Adding TRE to combined ENC and BIN resulted in an increase in the expression of cleaved PARP, BAK and p-H2AX protein, compared with ENC/BIN. (A, B) Adding TRE to ENC/BIN decreased the expression of p-MEK at 72 h after treatment, but did not decrease the expression of p-ERK at 4, 24, and 72 h after treatment. (C) Adding TRE to ENC/BIN significantly downregulated p-AKT expression in RKO, but not in HT29. (D) Adding TRE to ENC/BIN significantly increased the protein expression of cleaved PARP at 72 h after treatment. (E) Adding TRE to ENC/BIN increased the expression of BAK and p-H2AX at 72 h after treatment.
Enhancement of the antiproliferative effect observed when retinoid is added to ENC/BIN is mediated in part by RARalpha or RXRalpha

Retinoids have been reported to have an antiproliferative effect in various tumors as agonists against RARalpha or RXRalpha. When TRE isomerizes into 9-cis retinoic acid, it acts as an agonist for RXR and also as a ligand for RAR. To evaluate the mechanism for the enhancement of the antiproliferative effect observed when adding TRE to ENC/BIN involved RARalpha or RXRalpha, we assessed the relation of the endogenous protein expression of RARalpha or RXRalpha with the synergistic antiproliferative effect of TRE. Endogenous expression of RARalpha was detected in RKO cells, but was very low or almost undetectable in the other five cell lines (Figure 4A). Endogenous expression of RXRalpha was highest in WiDr cells, with expression declining, in order, in HT29, LIM2405, RKO, COLO205, and Co-115 cells (Figure 4A), indicating that the degree of endogenous RARalpha and RXRalpha expression did not correlate with the level of the TRE-induced synergistic enhancement of the antiproliferative effect.

Adding TRE to combined ENC and BIN resulted in the induction of RARalpha- or RXRalpha-mediated apoptosis. (A) Endogenous RARalpha and RXRalpha expressions did not correlate with the response to TRE combined with ENC/BIN. (B) Transfection of RKO cells with si-RARalpha and si-RXRalpha suppressed RARalpha and RXRalpha expressions respectively at 72 h after transfection. (C) Transfection of HT29 cells with si-RXRalpha suppressed the protein expression of RXRalpha. HT29 cells without endogenous RARalpha expression were treated only with si-NC and si-RXRalpha. (D) When RARalpha or RXRalpha was silenced, the enhancement observed when TRE was added to ENC/BIN decreased in RKO cells. (E) When RXRalpha was silenced, the enhancement observed when bexarotene (BEX) was added to ENC/BIN was partly canceled in RKO cells. (F, G) When RXRalpha was silenced, the enhancement observed when TRE or BEX was added to ENC/BIN was partly canceled in HT29 cells. (H) When RARalpha or RXRalpha was silenced, the enhancing cleaved PARP protein expression observed when TRE was added to ENC/BIN/CET in RKO cells was canceled. Results are presented as means +- SEM. *p < 0.05, **p < 0.001.

We next aimed to elucidate whether enhancement of the antiproliferative effect exerted by TRE is affected by alterations in the expression of RARalpha or RXRalpha. Considering that only RXRalpha is endogenously expressed in BRAF V600E CRC cells, except in RKO, we used both the RAR and RXR agonist TRE and the selective RXR agonist BEX for all cell lines. At 72 h after transfection with si-RARalpha and si-RXRalpha, the protein expression of RARalpha and RXRalpha was reduced in RKO cells (39% and 87% respectively; Figure 4B). In HT29 cells, which lack endogenous RARalpha expression, we used only siRNA against RXRalpha and confirmed reduced expression of RXRalpha (by 60%; Figure 4A,C). When the expression of RARalpha and RXRalpha was reduced, the enhancement of the antiproliferative effect observed with TRE/ENC/BIN in RKO was inhibited (Figure 4D). The enhancement of the antiproliferative effect observed when BEX was added to ENC/BIN was canceled, at least in part, only when RXRalpha expression was reduced (Figure 4E). The reduced expression of RXRalpha partly inhibited the enhancement of the antiproliferative effect observed with the addition of TRE or BEX to ENC/BIN in HT29 and RKO cells alike (Figure 4F,G). Next, we validated the similar reduction of enhancement of the antiproliferative effect by the addition of TRE to ENC/CET and ENC/BIN/CET in RKO cells (Figure S10A). These results indicated that, at least in part, mediation of RARalpha or RXRalpha stimulation by TRE and BEX enhances the antiproliferative effect. Then, to confirm that the RARalpha- or RXRalpha-mediated enhancement of the antiproliferative effect observed when TRE is added to ENC/BIN leads to apoptosis, we assessed cleaved PARP expression in RKO cells transfected with si-NC, si-RARalpha, or si-RXRalpha. When either RARalpha or RXRalpha was silenced, the cleaved PARP expression that had increased with the addition of TRE to ENC/BIN or ENC/BIN/CET decreased (Figures 4H and S10B). Taken together, our results indicated that the addition of TRE to ENC/BIN, with or without CET, exerts a synergistic antiproliferative effect, at least in part, through RARalpha- or RXRalpha-mediated apoptosis.
TRE, when added to ENC/CET or ENC/BIN/CET, inhibited tumor growth in vivo

To validate in vivo the antitumor effect and toxicity of the addition of TRE to ENC/BIN/CET but also to ENC/CET, another current standard therapy for BRAF V600E CRC, we used a xenograft mouse model. Tumor volume was significantly smaller in the TRE/ENC/CET group than in the ENC/CET group and in the TRE/ENC/BIN/CET group than in the ENC/BIN/CET group; no significant difference between vehicle or TRE alone was evident (Figure 5A). Tumor volume did not significantly differ between ENC/BIN/CET group and TRE/ENC/CET group, nor between the TRE/ENC/CET group and TRE/ENC/BIN/CET group. Mild dry skin was observed on all mice treated with tretinoin. At 28 days, body weight did not significantly differ between the groups treated with or without TRE (Figure 5B). To evaluate differences in cell proliferation between the groups treated with and without TRE, we determined the Ki-67 labeling index in resected tumor tissues. No significant differences in the Ki-67 labeling index were evident between the vehicle group and the TRE alone group; however, the Ki-67 labeling index was significantly lower in the TRE/ENC/CET and TRE/ENC/BIN/CET groups than in the ENC/CET and ENC/BIN/CET groups (Figure 5C,D). Taken together, those results indicated that the addition of TRE to ENC/CET or ENC/BIN/CET was associated with synergistic antitumor effects in vivo as well as in vitro.

Tumor volumes are presented as means in cubic millimeters +- standard deviation. (B) Mouse body weight was measured every 3 days. (C, D) Anti-Ki-67 antibody immunohistochemical staining of live cells from resected tumor tissue of each treatment. Results are presented as means +- SD. *p < 0.05.
DISCUSSION

In this study, we identified compounds that would enhance the antitumor effect of combined therapy with BRAF inhibitor, MEK inhibitor, and anti-EGFR antibody in BRAF V600E CRC. To the best of our knowledge, this report is the first to demonstrate that retinoids, including TRE, synergistically enhance the antiproliferative effect of BRAF and MEK inhibitors in BRAF V600E CRC. In addition, the enhancement of the antiproliferative effect was demonstrated to operate, at least in part, through RARalpha- or RXRalpha-mediated apoptosis, and TRE enhances the antitumor effect of BRAF inhibitor and anti-EGFR antibody with or without MEK inhibitor in vivo.

In current clinical practice, TRE and TAM are used in the treatment of acute promyelocytic leukemia, and BEX is used for cutaneous T cell lymphoma. Few studies have explored the therapeutic potential of retinoids in solid tumors. Several studies have analyzed the ability of retinoids to inhibit the proliferation of CRC cells in vitro or in vivo. Several clinical trials have analyzed the efficacy of treatments combining a retinoid with other drugs in CRC. However, the efficacy of these combinations has not been validated in randomized studies. The specific effects of TRE on BRAF V600E CRC cells and the clinical role of TRE in patients with BRAF V600E CRC remain unclear. Our study demonstrated that TRE enhances the antitumor effect of BRAF, MEK, and EGFR inhibition on BRAF V600E CRC. The addition of TRE to a current standard therapeutic regimen of BRAF inhibitor, MEK inhibitor, and anti-EGFR antibody could be a new strategy for patients with BRAF V600E CRC. In addition, TRE is expected to have synergistic efficacy when TRE is combined with not only a BRAF-targeted therapy, but also a combination of BRAF-targeted therapy and cytotoxic agents, or BRAF-targeted therapy and immune checkpoint inhibitors. Azarifar et al. suggested that TRE suppressed the self-renewal capability of cancer stem cells and can increase the therapeutic efficiency of 5-FU. TRE, which may enhance the efficacy of a combination of BRAF-targeted therapy and cytotoxic agents. Next, targeting MDSCs is an attractive strategy to enhance the efficacy of immunotherapies. TRE acts on MDSCs to promote their differentiation and leads to decreased frequency of circulation MDSCs via ERK1/2 activation, glutathione synthase upregulation, and glutathione generation. A phase Ib/II clinical trial, which evaluated the safety and efficacy of the combination of TRE with pembrolizumab in patients with melanoma, has shown that the combination therapy had favorable tolerability and high response rate. In addition, Tobin et al. reported that TRE decreases MDSC immunosuppressive gene expression and immunosuppressive function, and suggested that the combination of TRE with immunotherapies represents a promising strategy to improve outcomes in cancer patients. Oncogenic BRAF can induce changes that facilitate tumor immune escape, and the inhibition of BRAF is associated with significant immunological changes in the tumor microenvironment that are considered favorable for antitumor immunity. Cooper et al. reported that immune checkpoint blockade using anti-PD-1 or anti-PD-L1 synergizes with BRAF-targeted therapy in an in vivo model. These combination therapies with TRE could be another promising strategy that has to be explored in future studies.

There is a significant association between the BRAF V600E mutation and MSI in CRC. MSI-high tumors are more immunogenic than other tumor subtypes, as the truncated proteins resulting from errors in unrepaired DNA strands function as neoantigens that activate the immune system. The KEYNOTE-177 study demonstrated that a BRAF mutation was not significantly associated with the worse survival of patients with MSI-high CRC treated with pembrolizumab. Conversely, patients with BRAF V600E and MSI-stable CRC have been associated with a poor prognosis, raising high potential medical needs particularly for treating patients with MSI-stable and BRAF V600E and MSI-stable CRC. In our study, the synergistic effect of the addition of TRE to BRAF, MEK, and EGFR inhibition was observed in RKO cells characterized with BRAF V600E and MSI-high and BRAF V600E, as well as in HT29 cells characterized with BRAF V600E and MSI-stable, which demonstrated that TRE enhanced the antitumor effect of BRAF, MEK, and EGFR inhibition on BRAF V600E CRC, regardless of MSI status.

The activity of retinoids is mediated primarily by members of the RAR and RXR subfamily. RARs form heterodimers with RXRs, while RXRs form heterodimers with various nuclear receptor superfamily members. The RXR dimers can be divided into the RXR homodimer, permissive heterodimers, and non-permissive heterodimers. The RXR homodimer and the permissive heterodimers become transcriptionally active in the sole presence of an RXR-selective ligand. In contrast, the non-permissive heterodimers are unresponsive to an RXR agonist alone. RAR/RXR is interestingly categorized as a non-permissive heterodimer. Our study indicated that not only TRE, but also the selective RXR agonist BEX, was associated with the synergistic enhancement of the antiproliferative effect of ENC/BIN, in part through an RXRalpha-mediated pathway. This suggests that the synergistic antiproliferative effect mediates a pathway activated by RXRalpha stimulation alone. Dillard et al. reported that, in vitro, RET increased the RXR-mediated proteasomal degradation of beta-catenin in TRE-resistant CRC cells, reducing the transcription of both exogenous and endogenous beta-catenin target genes. In both in vitro and in vivo models, Cesario et al. demonstrated that the activation of the RXR/PPARgamma permissive heterodimer inhibited CRC cell growth. Our results in the present study, demonstrating that retinoids can potentially synergistically enhance the antiproliferative effect mediated by an RXRalpha-only mechanism, are consistent with the earlier reports. Furthermore, we demonstrated that a selective RAR agonist TAM enhances the antiproliferative effect of ENC/BIN and that reduced expression of RARalpha canceled the enhancement of the antiproliferative effect of ENC/BIN in RKO cells. The latter result suggests that an RARalpha-only mechanism also exists. Further studies are needed to elucidate the exact mechanisms that underlie the synergistic enhancement effect of TRE.

Our data indicate that the Bcl-2 family is involved in TRE enhancement of the antiproliferative effect of ENC/BIN. BAK and BAX are the pro-apoptotic effector proteins of the Bcl-2 family. Several in vitro studies have shown that a retinoid antiproliferative effect on CRC cells is mediated by Bcl-2 family proteins. Furthermore, the synergistic induction of apoptosis by inhibition of the Bcl-2 and MEK/MAPK pathways has been clarified in various tumors. For instance, a potentially therapeutic MAPK-targeted therapy, combined with inhibition of Bcl-2 family member Mcl-1 for BRAF V600E CRC, has been proposed based on the results from an in vitro model. Our observations, that the mechanism of TRE's synergistic enhancement of the antiproliferative effect of ENC/BIN is mediated in part through Bcl-2 protein family-associated apoptosis, are in line with those previous findings.

In summary, using an in vitro BRAF V600E CRC model, we first demonstrated that TRE synergistically enhances the antiproliferative effect of BRAF and MEK inhibition at least in part by activating RXRalpha- or RARalpha-mediated apoptosis. Subsequently, we demonstrated in vivo that TRE synergistically enhances the antitumor effect of either BRAF and EGFR inhibition or of BRAF, MEK, and EGFR inhibition. Our findings suggest the possibility of developing a novel therapeutic strategy for patients with BRAF V600E CRC, whose prognosis is poorer than that of their counterparts with other molecular CRC subtypes.

passages.text: Human breast tissue engineering in health and disease

The human mammary gland represents a highly organized and dynamic tissue, uniquely characterized by postnatal developmental cycles. During pregnancy and lactation, it undergoes extensive hormone-stimulated architectural remodeling, culminating in the formation of specialized structures for milk production to nourish offspring. Moreover, it carries significant health implications, due to the high prevalence of breast cancer. Therefore, gaining insight into the unique biology of the mammary gland can have implications for managing breast cancer and promoting the well-being of both women and infants. Tissue engineering techniques hold promise to narrow the translational gap between existing breast models and clinical outcomes. Here, we provide an overview of the current landscape of breast tissue engineering, outline key requirements, and the challenges to overcome for achieving more predictive human breast models. We propose methods to validate breast function and highlight preclinical applications for improved understanding and targeting of breast cancer. Beyond mammary gland physiology, representative human breast models can offer new insight into stem cell biology and developmental processes that could extend to other organs and clinical contexts.
Introduction
Key features of mammary gland biology and how they could be recapitulated through tissue engineering technologies.

The cellular compartments which need to be considered consist of the functional mammary epithelium comprised of luminal and basal epithelial cells, the stroma comprising mammary fibroblasts, adipocytes and immune cells, as well as the vasculature. These cellular compartments can be addressed using cell lines or primary cell sources such as patient/donor-derived organoids. The non-cellular microenvironment consists of a network of extracellular matrix components, which can be mimicked using specifically tailored hydrogels. Bioengineering techniques, such as bioprinting and organ-on-a-chip technology, enable the fabrication of recapitulative tissue architectures and help mimic crucial stimuli, such as flow and nutrient/hormone supply, to achieve full tissue maturation and functionality.

The human breast performs the important function of nourishing offspring and promotes infant microbiome health and immune function. Despite these essential tasks, our knowledge of human mammary gland biology and pathology remains incomplete. This includes our understanding of breast cancer, one of the most frequent cancer-related deaths in women (Siegel et al,). Representative in vitro models of breast tissue are needed to narrow this knowledge gap and support the development of new, effective therapies for breast cancer. Mouse models (Wagner,) and human mammary epithelial cell (MEC) lines (Qu et al,) have long been the gold standard for mammary gland research. Mouse models do provide a high degree of tissue complexity, and the possibility to study systemic interactions and treatment effects. However, they offer only limited representation of human breast function, due to interspecies differences in architecture, stromal composition, hormone levels, duration of lactation, and extent of involution (Medina,). At the same time, the intricate connection of mammary gland function with its three-dimensional (3D) organization has long been recognized through pioneering work showing that alveoli formation and milk expression is tightly linked to the presence and distribution of extracellular matrix (ECM), biomechanical cues and architectural guidance (Barcellos-Hoff et al,; Emerman and Pitelka,; Petersen et al,; Nelson et al,), which cannot be recapitulated in human 2D cell cultures. This strongly emphasizes the need for more representative human in vitro models that recapitulate 3D architecture. Organoids have emerged as important in vitro 3D tools for human modeling, showing some level of self-organization (Brassard and Lutolf,; Clevers,; Drost and Clevers,; Simian and Bissell,; Sato et al,). However, their higher-scale architectural complexity is still limited and variability in phenotype and cellular composition can hinder experimental, and especially drug-screening, applications (Rossi et al,). Bioengineering offers a valuable technology for introducing more complex and reproducible structures and cellular organization in in vitro tissue models. Here, we review how different tissue engineering strategies can help to mimic the unique features of the human breast in vitro. We discuss the specific needs for ECM engineering and recapitulation of tissue-like architecture (Fig. 1) and highlight the potential of such engineered models for improving the clinical management of breast cancer. Finally, we address the maturation and validation strategies required to meet this goal (Fig. 1).
Intricate interplay of cell composition, tissue architecture, and hormonal regulation
Architectural structure of the mammary gland and how it is hormonally regulated during various cycles of development.

A rudimental ductal tree comprised of a bilayered epithelium that already exists during fetal development, under the influence of various hormones, continues to expand during puberty, and undergoes dynamic changes throughout each menstrual cycle. In the case of pregnancy, rising levels of estrogen, progesterone, and prolactin lead to the maturation of the mammary gland into fully functional multilayered alveoli. After birth, sudden drops in estrogen and progesterone levels, as well as alternating stimulation through oxytocin and prolactin, enable milk production and secretion. Under the influence of MMPs and leptin, the mammary gland undergoes involution to a pre-pregnancy state after weaning.

The mammary gland is composed of a ductal tree branching into secondary and tertiary ducts that end in terminal ductal lobular units (TDLUs), considered the functional units of the mature human mammary gland (Dontu and Ince,). The ductal parts are characterized by an epithelial bilayer, with luminal cells composing the ductal inner layer and basal cells residing on the outer layer. Luminal cells are responsible for milk production, while basal cells can differentiate into myoepithelial cells that enable contraction and, thereby, discharge and transport of milk during lactation. In contrast to this bilayered organization in the duct, in the terminally differentiated TDLUs, luminal epithelial cells are multilayered to enable efficient milk production (Fig. 2) (Macias and Hinck,; Slepicka et al,). These structures are highly vascularized to ensure a sufficient supply of nutrients, hormones, and immune cells and embedded in a fibroblast-rich adipose stroma, which provides further architectural support and nutrient supply (Macias and Hinck,; Dziegelewska and Gajewska,). Stromal fibroblasts critically contribute to mammary gland branching morphogenesis, and their diverse roles in this process and functional heterogeneity have been extensively reviewed elsewhere (Sumbal et al,). While the mammary gland contains a population of tissue-resident, ductal macrophages involved in tissue integrity and homeostasis (Dawson et al,), CSF-1-recruited macrophages also play a role and promote mammary gland branching morphogenesis (Nguyen and Pollard,; Gouon-Evans et al,). Adding further temporal complexity to this spatial and cellular regulation and organization, the functional maturation of the human breast is tightly regulated by stromal-produced growth factors, as well as hormonal cues provided by the pituitary gland and the ovaries (Slepicka et al,; Hannan et al,; Macias and Hinck,). As an example of this complexity involving multiple factors and cell types, estrogen-stimulated macrophages enhance fibroblast proliferation and invasion through TNFalpha and matrix metalloproteinase (MMP) 9 secretion, which then provides a larger stromal bed to allow for epithelial cell proliferation and structure formation (Fleming et al,). Thus, the mammary gland is complexly regulated through an interplay of various cell types, their spatial organization, and hormonal and growth factor stimulation. Highly unique to the mammary gland, as opposed to other organs, this altogether cumulates in extensive tissue remodeling during postnatal developmental cycles (Fig. 2).
Mammary gland developmental stages

A rudimentary ductal tree already establishes in utero guided by FGF and Wnt signaling (Slepicka et al,). However, during puberty, aided by paracrine signaling of stromal cells and under the influence of multiple hormones, such as gonadotropin, estrogen, progesterone, growth hormone, and IGF1, elongation, branching, and bud formation take place (Slepicka et al,; Macias and Hinck,). This includes a role for eotaxin-recruited eosinophils (Gouon-Evans et al,) and mast cells through serine proteases (Lilla and Werb,) in this pubertal morphogenesis. During each estrous cycle, alveologenesis and mammary tissue expansion prepare the mammary gland for a potential pregnancy. In the case of pregnancy, progesterone, prolactin, IGF1, and insulin regulate MEC proliferation and terminal secretory differentiation of TDLUs into functional alveoli (Slepicka et al,). Mediated by a postpartum drop in progesterone levels, the production of milk is initiated and oxytocin, as well as mechanical stimulation of a suckling newborn, enable milk secretion (Macias and Hinck,). Upon cessation of breastfeeding, prolactin levels drop, milk-producing cells die and become phagocytosed by ductal macrophages (Dawson et al,), and MMP-mediated tissue remodeling takes place (Hannan et al,; Slepicka et al,). Finally, an increase in leptin leads to adipogenesis, replacing the secretory epithelium with adipocytes (Zwick et al,), completing this involution process and returning the mammary gland to its pre-pregnancy state (Hannan et al,; Slepicka et al,).
Mammary gland extracellular matrix represents a complex and dynamic environment

Next to the cellular and structural changes described in the previous section and summarized in Fig. 2, the non-cellular compartment of the mammary gland strongly impacts its morphogenesis and functionality (Rauner et al,) and is dynamically regulated as well (Schedin and Keely,). It, thereby, forms a critical aspect to take into account in mammary gland modeling approaches to guide cell organization.
Of mice and women

While limited compared to studies in mouse model systems, analysis on human breast ECM has been done for, example, by Gusterson et al looking at the positional relationship between myoepithelial cells and basement membrane (Gusterson et al,) and by Keller et al comparing the spatial distribution of collagen-I in human breast tissue, human-derived decellularized breast tissue, collagen-1 hydrogels, and Matrigel. They could identify mesh-like and long fibrous ECM organization and loss of this specific texture in ductal carcinoma samples. This interconnected fibrous network was maintained in dECM-derived hydrogels, while interconnectivity could not be observed in regular collagen-1 hydrogels. In addition, they observed a 5.7-fold increase in ECM stiffness in tumor samples compared to normal breast tissue (Keller et al,), a mechanical property of breast tissue that is commonly used as a parameter for cancer detection (Ramiao et al,). Also, in a healthy situation, the mechanical properties of breast tissue can show dynamic alterations. The collective motion of epithelial cells, for instance, induces local tension and mechanical response of the surrounding collagen, which plays a role in ductal elongation (Buchmann et al,). However, the majority of our knowledge on breast ECM composition and function is derived from mouse data, as further detailed below. It is important to note that, despite many similarities, there are also substantial interspecies differences in ECM composition, exemplified by the complete absence of intralobular stroma in mice, as opposed to humans (Dontu and Ince,). This signifies a need to carefully consider the origin of ECM components for mammary gland modeling and assess whether data on ECM composition or spatial organization can be translated from mouse to human.
Mammary ECM composition

The mammary epithelium is lined by a thin basement membrane mainly made up of collagen-IV and laminins (Yurchenco and Patton,). This basement membrane, produced by myoepithelial cells (Gudjonsson et al,) and stromal fibroblasts (Muschler and Streuli,), is a key regulator of the integrin-mediated polarized mammary epithelial phenotype. Particularly, laminin-III and collagen-IV are responsible for maintaining tissue polarity (Muschler and Streuli,; Nelson and Bissell,; Insua-Rodriguez and Oskarsson,; Schedin and Keely,). The surrounding ECM is characterized by a looser network of an interstitial fibrous collagen-rich matrix, including collagens-I and -III, proteoglycans, hyaluronic acid (HA), fibronectin, tenascins, and various matrix remodeling enzymes (e.g., MMPs) (Insua-Rodriguez and Oskarsson,; Muschler and Streuli,).
Dynamic ECM changes during mammary gland development

The composition of the mammary ECM varies strongly during the different mammary gland developmental stages described above, as extensive remodeling takes place to allow the cells to branch from primary to secondary ducts, or to form TDLUs, and regress again during involution (Insua-Rodriguez and Oskarsson,; Muschler and Streuli,). For instance, when ductal elongation occurs during puberty, the basement membrane of terminal end buds (TEBs; transient structures found in the pubertal gland) is thinning, rich in HA, and does not contain collagen-I bundles (Schedin and Keely,). The surrounding ECM presents with collagen fibers radiating away from these TEBs, facilitating tissue growth from the tips (Ingman et al,). Finally, the basement membrane adjacent to ductal parts is actually rich in collagen-I, where no outgrowth occurs (Silberstein and Daniel,). These findings in mice clearly demonstrate; (1) the various changes occurring in ECM composition during puberty, (2) that these alterations are spatially restricted, and (3) how this topography of dynamic ECM composition directs ductal elongation and branching. During lactation, generally less fibrous ECM proteins (e.g. collagens) can be observed, providing a compliant environment for MECs to fully mature, while during involution, these components are again increased (Schedin et al,).
Cancer-associated dynamic ECM alterations

ECM remodeling also takes place during breast cancer progression. Changes in protein make-up, such as through downregulation of laminin-III and upregulation of MMPs, lead to basement membrane disruption and degradation, causing a loss in epithelial polarity and enabling invasiveness of the tumor (Schedin and Keely,; Nelson and Bissell,; Muschler and Streuli,; Insua-Rodriguez and Oskarsson,). At the same time, laminin-332, which promotes tumor progression through anchorage-independent survival, is upregulated (Insua-Rodriguez and Oskarsson,). Overall, breast tumorigenesis is accompanied by desmoplasia; increased matrix protein deposition (especially fibrillar collagens) and remodeling, resulting in an increase of ECM density and stiffness promoting metastatic behavior and correlating with poor treatment outcomes (Insua-Rodriguez and Oskarsson,; Schedin and Keely,). These changes in matrix composition and density during breast cancer progression, such as proteolysis of basement membrane proteins following MMP upregulation, share a lot of similarities to the changes occurring during involution, explaining the temporarily increased risk and poor prognosis of breast cancer postpartum (Lyons et al,; McDaniel et al,; Schedin et al,). In contrast, during lactation, deposition of fibrillar collagen-I is reduced, correlating with a reduced risk of breast cancer through breastfeeding, which decreases even more upon prolonged breastfeeding (4.3% for every 12 months of breastfeeding) (Maller et al,; Takabatake et al,; Stordal,). Because of its many facets influencing mammary gland development and pathology, it is clear that exploiting the ECM to guide functional cell organization in in vitro models is not only reliant on the spatial availability of different matrix proteins, but also on their biomechanical properties and their ability to be dynamically remodeled.

Various strategies have been implemented to culture normal and cancerous MECs in different natural ECM components, as briefly summarized in Table 1. While these approaches using different single ECM components were successful to some degree, it is becoming more and more evident, that relying on a single-material approach might not yield fully functional breast models. Therefore, the focus is shifting towards multimaterial approaches. An example is the work of Nguyen-Ngoc et al, who cultured murine primary MECs in Matrigel or a mix of Matrigel and collagen-I. (Nguyen-Ngoc et al,). In mixed gels, they observed a more faithful recapitulation of branching and TEB formation (e.g., bifurcation and myoepithelial coverage during bud initiation/elongation) than in Matrigel, whereas collagen-I only induced an invasive phenotype that could be restored by the cells own basement membrane production. Extended branching and endbud formation could be reproduced for mouse mammary gland organoids (MGOs) in floating collagen-Matrigel gels (Qu et al,), a culture method already pioneered by Emerman and Pitelka in 1977 (Emerman and Pitelka,). However, this induced only little branching and bud elongation in human iPSC-derived MGOs, suggesting a requirement for a more complex ECM composition for human MECs. This was confirmed by Sokol et al, who cultured primary human MECs in a multimaterial matrix containing natural collagen-I, laminin, fibronectin, and hyaluronan, and observed self-organization, expansion, and differentiation into near-mature mammary tissues comprised of ductal and lobular morphologies with correct polarization (Sokol et al,). Furthermore, the resulting structures responded to hormonal stimulation with lumen formation and induction of lipid droplet production. While even in this mixed gel, complex ductal and lobular morphologies did not occur very frequently, they were never observed in case Matrigel only, or only polymerized collagen was used to grow the cells. Rauner et al recently used this multimaterial matrix to yield human breast 3D structures through directed organogenesis rather than spontaneous self-assembly usually observed in BME (Rauner et al,). Together, these results emphasize the impact of ECM complexity on cellular organization and function and indicate that the optimal ECM composition can differ between mouse and human breast tissue. Further knowledge on human ECM composition and its dynamic changes during the development of complex architectures will be necessary to mimic breast morphogenesis in vitro. Such a comprehensive map of the human breast ECM during different developmental stages could guide biomaterial engineering to build near-physiological matrices for advanced in vitro modeling.
Decellularized extracellular matrix
Approaches to guide MEC behavior through biomaterial engineering.

Shape-fidelity post-fabrication and cell function often impose opposing requirements on biomaterials. Strategies to achieve both, include the modification of materials with high shape fidelity to enhance bioactivity, or the modification of bioactive materials to enhance shape fidelity. Positioning within the Biofabrication Window does not imply qualitative classification of the used materials, but points towards the direction of improvement the presented research aims to achieve. While multimaterial approaches show superiority for modeling human mammary gland morphogenesis, these approaches yield a random distribution of only a selection of ECM proteins. A possibility to retain not only tissue-specific native ECM composition, but also spatial arrangement is the use of tissue-derived decellularized ECM (dECM). Depending on tissue type and size, as well as desired application, tissue pieces are objected to a series of physical (e.g., freezing or hydrostatic pressure), chemical (e.g., Triton X-100 or SDS), and enzymatical (e.g., trypsin) procedures to remove cells and lipids, to obtain a cell-free ECM (Mendibil et al,). Some of the more gentle approaches allow to retain the original tissue architecture, as demonstrated by Jin et al, who used human normal and cancerous tissue to produce decellularized scaffolds and reseed them with BC cells. While cancer-derived dECM induced epithelial- mesenchymal transition (EMT) and cancer cell proliferation, normal-derived dECM did not (Jin et al,). This demonstrates a strong functional influence, which was also shown for age-dependent changes in dECM. Compared to young murine dECM, dECM derived from old mice was sufficient to induce cancer-like behavior in normal MECs and promote invasiveness in cancerous cells, demonstrating a role for the ECM in increased breast cancer risk with advanced age (Bahcecioglu et al,). These profound functional consequences strongly argue that dECM provides the most accurate native tissue environment. However, because of interspecies differences, human tissue is needed to faithfully recapitulate the human breast ECM. While protocols are in place for processing human reduction mammoplasty and mastectomy material (LaBarge et al,), not all labs will have the required ethical approvals in place and easy access to these tissue sources. In addition, although some decellularization methods maintain tissue architecture, they do not allow control over it, making these approaches less suitable for engineering purposes. Therefore, most tissue engineering technologies opt for more disruptive protocols to produce hydrogels from decellularized matrix proteins. Here, the composition and proportions of ECM components are maintained, but the structure and spatial distribution is lost (Mendibil et al,). This could potentially be recovered by the utilization of biofabrication techniques. Additive manufacturing techniques, for instance, 3D bioprinting could reintroduce architecture through the spatially controlled deposition of hydrogel, but also living cells and molecules (Groll et al,). However, when applying ECM components in such a bioprinting setting, their requirements for promoting optimal cell function often compete with the requirements posed by the fabrication modalities and desired shape fidelity. Many ECM components, such as collagen-I or laminin, are too soft to retain shape fidelity post printing at concentrations that allow for proper cell function, while many synthetic materials, such as poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG), which can easily be tailored to the desired mechanical properties, do not offer bioactive cues to promote cell viability and function. Therefore, many biofabrication approaches have been restricted to what has been termed the Biofabrication Window and moving out of this traditional window has been identified as one of the critical steps for the biofabrication field to progress toward more representative human tissue models. For now, biofabrication strategies are stuck in a range of material properties (concentration, stiffness, crosslinking density) that allow for only moderate shape fidelity to also ensure cell viability, making concessions on both critical aspects for effective tissue modeling (Malda et al,) (Fig. 3). Thus, additional developments are needed to yield printed tissue constructs that promote proper cell function, while maintaining high shape fidelity (Malda et al,). Multiple approaches to achieve this have been suggested, for instance, combining bioinks with poor structural integrity, but high bioactivity with a mechanically supportive material, or support baths, to enhance their shape fidelity during printing (Malda et al,; Levato et al,). In addition, bioink design is applied to make synthetic highly printable materials more compatible with cell viability and function, for instance, through the addition of cell signaling sequences, or enzymatically cleavable sequences. Reversibly, the printability and shape fidelity of natural polymers that already possess bioactive moieties can be improved by introducing new crosslinking chemistries or rheological tuning (Levato et al,; Malda et al,).
Development of bioprintable biomaterials

Zhang et al proposed a biocompatible gel made of oligo(ethylene glycol)-grafted polyisocyanides (PICs) as a synthetic hydrogel for murine MGO culture (Zhang et al,). To improve bioactivity, the gel was functionalized with the cell adhesion peptide RGD. Organoid formation efficiency was shown to be dependent on stiffness; with softer gels promoting higher organoid formation, compared to stiffer gels. In contrast, the cellular composition was influenced by RGD-density and, thereby, the frequency of cell-matrix interactions; high-density RGD-gels led to an increased proportion of basal cells in MGO cultures (Zhang et al,). This modularity of PIC-based materials, enabling optimization to fabrication needs, as well as biological requirements, makes them attractive materials for biofabrication (Sanchez et al,). However, natural ECM components contain far more than just adhesive peptides to guide cell behavior. Identifying the full spectrum of tissue-specific bioactive sequences and their required spatial distributions to generate fully ECM-mimicking synthetic materials poses a challenging task. Therefore, the modification of natural polymers that already possess these properties is another path toward fabrication-suitable bioactive materials. This is, for instance, confirmed by Bock et al, who compared synthetic to natural:but modified:biomaterials for the growth of BC organoids (Bock et al,). This work showed that the use of GelSH, thiolated gelatin, a natural collagen-derived polymer that can be crosslinked to enhance shape fidelity, resulted in the most complex and large growing BC organoids, as compared to traditionally used biomaterials. Moreover, the authors highlight future perspectives on the use of GelSH for precision medicine applications, where the gel stiffness can potentially be modulated to fit the tumor of origin (Bock et al,). Protease-degradable crosslinkers have been introduced into an HA-based hydrogel to consider the need for cells to be able to remodel their microenvironment, which resulted in endothelial cells sprouting towards an angiogenic gradient (Song et al,). Together, these approaches show the potential of modifying synthetic and natural polymers to improve tissue function during fabrication. However, most of these approaches still make concessions between either printing accuracy or bioactivity, which has sparked the development of even more advanced biomaterials. For instance, Skardal et al composed bioinks compatible with extrusion-based bioprinting by combining dECM from different tissues with HA, gelatine-based hydrogels, and PEG-based crosslinkers, yielding tissue products of a wide range of stiffnesses that contained the bioactive components of the tissues' native ECM (Skardal et al,). For breast tissue, a similar approach has been applied to improve the print fidelity of dECM by the addition of collagen-I (Blanco-Fernandez et al,). Bioactive properties can also be advanced by the controlled release of, or grafting, of cell favorable components, such as growth factors. Selectively photo-grafting of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) into a print made of gelatine-norbonene was able to direct sprouting of endothelial cells into the surrounding tissue (Falandt et al,). Similarly, Fisher et al photografted EGF onto a HA-based hydrogel and showed that it preferentially directed BC cell invasion into the tissue in relation to the expression of EGF receptor (EGFR) on the cell lines used (Fisher et al,). More recently, the generation of supramolecular materials that employ non-covalent bonds has gained much attention, due to the possibility of cells to break bonds to migrate and expand in the material, while shape fidelity can be maintained (Mihajlovic et al,).
